distractorNotes.b: 768 CSS pixels represents a tablet portrait view, not the 320 CSS pixel reflow standard.
distractorNotes.c: 1024 CSS pixels is standard desktop/tablet resolution, not the 400% zoom / 320 CSS px reflow test condition.

sourceNote: W3C Understanding SC 1.4.10 Reflow defines 320 CSS px (400% zoom at 1280px) without two-dimensional scrolling.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.8 (Target Size (Minimum)), what is the minimum target dimension for pointer inputs?

options.text: At least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, unless an exception such as sufficient spacing perimeter applies.
At least 44 by 44 CSS pixels across all controls without any allowed spacing offset exemptions.
At least 48 by 48 physical hardware device pixels measured on the native display screen.
At least 12 by 12 CSS pixels for inline hyperlinks and interactive header menu buttons.

explanation: WCAG 2.2 introduced SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) at Level AA, requiring targets to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except where spacing perimeter, inline text, user agent defaults, or essential presentations apply. (In contrast, SC 2.5.5 Target Size at Level AAA requires 44 by 44 CSS pixels).

distractorNotes.b: 44 by 44 CSS pixels is the enhanced Level AAA threshold in SC 2.5.5, not the Level AA minimum in SC 2.5.8.
distractorNotes.c: WCAG specifications measure target sizes in CSS pixels, not variable physical hardware device pixels.
distractorNotes.d: 12 by 12 CSS pixels is too small and fails both Level AA and Level AAA target size requirements.

sourceNote: W3C Understanding SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) establishes 24x24 CSS pixels minimum at Level AA.

stem: In the Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG) 2.0, how is the scope divided between Part A and Part B?

options.text: Part A governs native desktop editing software applications, while Part B governs web-based content management platforms.
Part A ensures the authoring tool UI is accessible, while Part B ensures the tool supports generating accessible web content.
Part A establishes normative technical conformance criteria, while Part B specifies non-normative advisory techniques.
Part A covers automated accessibility evaluation engines, while Part B governs manual rich text authoring environments.

explanation: ATAG 2.0 is structured into two main parts: Part A focuses on making the authoring tool user interface itself accessible to authors with disabilities (following WCAG principles for software). Part B focuses on supporting the authoring tool's ability to produce accessible web content (enabling, preserving, and checking accessibility).

distractorNotes.a: ATAG 2.0 applies across both desktop and web-based authoring software; its division into parts is based on tool UI accessibility versus output accessibility, not software platform.
distractorNotes.c: Both Part A and Part B contain normative success criteria as well as non-normative techniques; the division separates tool UI accessibility from content production support.
distractorNotes.d: Automated evaluation features and manual authoring interfaces are both covered under Part B (guidelines B.2, B.3, and B.4) rather than split across parts.

sourceNote: W3C ATAG 2.0 §Structure defines Part A (accessible tool UI) and Part B (supporting accessible content generation).

stem: Under ATAG 2.0 Guideline B.2, what requirement must an authoring tool satisfy when converting content between formats?

options.text: It must require the author to manually re-enter all alternative text and structural metadata after conversion.
It must translate non-standard markup elements into proprietary tool-specific metadata tags.
It must preserve accessibility information (such as alt text and heading structure) during content transformations.
It must generate an external conformance claim document certifying the target format conforms to WCAG.

explanation: ATAG 2.0 Guideline B.2 requires authoring tools to preserve accessibility information during content transformations, conversions, and migrations. For example, when converting a document from a word processing format to HTML or PDF, alternative text, headings, table structures, and language tags must be retained.

distractorNotes.a: ATAG B.2 mandates automated preservation of existing accessibility information during conversion.
distractorNotes.b: Authoring tools must output standard accessible web content rather than proprietary markup formats.
distractorNotes.d: Guideline B.2 focuses on preserving document accessibility data, not generating conformance claim files.

sourceNote: W3C ATAG 2.0 Guideline B.2 mandates preserving accessibility information during content transformations.

stem: In the European standard EN 301 549, how are the accessibility requirements for web content in Chapter 9 determined?

options.text: By defining a separate set of proprietary European Union accessibility rules distinct from W3C standards.
By referencing United States Section 508 standards without incorporating any international criteria.
By mandating that all web content must satisfy WCAG 2.1 Level AAA success criteria without exceptions.
By directly adopting and harmonizing with the W3C WCAG 2.1 Level A and Level AA success criteria.

explanation: Chapter 9 of EN 301 549 ('Web') directly harmonizes with and adopts W3C WCAG 2.1 Level A and Level AA success criteria as its technical accessibility requirements for web pages and web applications across European public and private procurement.

distractorNotes.a: EN 301 549 explicitly harmonizes with W3C WCAG rather than creating competing proprietary European rules.
distractorNotes.b: EN 301 549 is a European EN standard harmonized with W3C WCAG, not a copy of US Section 508.
distractorNotes.c: EN 301 549 requires Level A and Level AA conformance; Level AAA is not legally mandated.

sourceNote: ETSI EN 301 549 Chapter 9 adopts W3C WCAG 2.1 Level AA as normative requirements for web content.

stem: According to the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) Accordion pattern, what is the recommended structure for an accordion header?

options.text: <button> wrapped inside a heading element
options.hintText: wraps an interactive toggle inside a structural heading element

options.text: Heading element nested inside <button>
options.hintText: nests a structural heading element inside an interactive button

options.text: <div> with role="button" and role="heading"
options.hintText: assigns conflicting ARIA roles to a generic container

options.text: Heading element with role="button"
options.hintText: assigns a button role directly to a heading element

explanation: In the APG Accordion pattern, each accordion header is structured as an HTML heading element containing an interactive button element. This ensures screen reader users can navigate the document structure via heading shortcuts while simultaneously accessing the interactive disclosure button.

distractorNotes.b: Nesting a heading inside a button is invalid HTML and prevents assistive technologies from exposing the heading in document outlines.
distractorNotes.c: Combining conflicting ARIA roles on a single div violates ARIA authoring rules and creates an ambiguous accessibility node.
distractorNotes.d: Applying role='button' directly to a heading element overrides native heading semantics, removing the heading from screen reader outline navigation.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Accordion pattern specifies wrapping interactive header buttons within appropriate heading elements.

stem: In an accessible accordion implementation, which ARIA attribute configuration on the accordion header button indicates that the associated section is currently visible?

options.text: aria-hidden="false" and aria-owns
options.hintText: indicates visibility in the accessibility tree and defines alternative parentage

options.text: aria-expanded="true" and aria-controls
options.hintText: indicates expanded disclosure state and references the controlled container

options.text: aria-selected="true" and aria-details
options.hintText: indicates selection state in selectable widgets and references extended details

options.text: aria-pressed="true" and aria-describedby
options.hintText: indicates toggle button pressed state and references descriptive text elements

explanation: The accordion header button must declare aria-expanded='true' when the corresponding panel is expanded and visible, and aria-expanded='false' when collapsed. The aria-controls attribute references the unique ID of the panel element controlled by the button.

distractorNotes.a: aria-hidden is used to remove elements from the accessibility tree, while aria-owns establishes parent-child hierarchy rather than disclosure state.
distractorNotes.c: aria-selected is specific to tab, gridcell, or option roles, and aria-details links to extended descriptions rather than expandable content.
distractorNotes.d: aria-pressed is used exclusively for toggle buttons, not for expanding or collapsing collapsible content panels.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Accordion pattern requires aria-expanded and aria-controls on the disclosure trigger button.

stem: In a WAI-ARIA 1.2 combobox widget, what is the effect of configuring aria-autocomplete='both' on the input element?

options.text: The input suggests completions inline within the text field without displaying a popup list.
The combobox displays a popup list of suggestions without inline completion in the input field.
Suggestions appear in a popup list and the first matching string completes the input field text.
The combobox accepts free-form text input while suppressing all automated predictive suggestions.

explanation: The aria-autocomplete property indicates whether user input triggers automatic display of predictions. The value 'both' indicates that matching suggestions are presented in a separate popup list and the most likely completion is inline-autocompleted directly within the input field.

distractorNotes.a: Inline text completion without a suggestion popup corresponds to aria-autocomplete='inline' rather than 'both'.
distractorNotes.b: Displaying popup suggestions without inline completion corresponds to aria-autocomplete='list' rather than 'both'.
distractorNotes.d: Suppressing all suggestions and autocompletion corresponds to aria-autocomplete='none' rather than 'both'.

sourceNote: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 §6.6 aria-autocomplete defines 'both' as providing both popup suggestion lists and inline text completion.

stem: In the WAI-ARIA 1.2 Combobox pattern, what attribute on the combobox input element identifies the popup listbox containing selectable options?

options.text: aria-owns
options.hintText: defines an alternative parent-child relationship in the accessibility tree

options.text: aria-haspopup
options.hintText: indicates the availability and type of interactive popup element

options.text: aria-activedescendant
options.hintText: identifies the currently active descendant element in a composite widget

options.text: aria-controls
options.hintText: identifies the element whose contents or presence are controlled by the current element

explanation: In WAI-ARIA 1.2, the combobox input element must declare role='combobox', aria-expanded to reflect open/closed state, and aria-controls pointing to the unique ID of the popup element (such as role='listbox') that it manages.

distractorNotes.a: While aria-owns was used in the legacy WAI-ARIA 1.0 combobox pattern, WAI-ARIA 1.2 requires aria-controls to identify the controlled popup.
distractorNotes.b: aria-haspopup communicates the type of popup (such as listbox), but does not identify the specific popup DOM element container by ID.
distractorNotes.c: aria-activedescendant identifies the currently highlighted or selected option item within the listbox, not the listbox container itself.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Combobox pattern requires aria-controls on the combobox input pointing to the popup listbox ID.

stem: In the WAI-ARIA APG Tabs pattern, how does automatic tab selection differ from manual tab selection?

options.text: In automatic selection, moving arrow key focus to a tab selects it and displays its associated panel.
In automatic selection, navigating between tabs with the Tab key activates each tab panel without arrows.
In automatic selection, arrow keys move focus among tabs while pressing Space or Enter activates the panel.
In automatic selection, selecting a tab immediately shifts keyboard focus into the tabpanel content area.

explanation: In automatic tab selection (selection follows focus), pressing the Right or Left Arrow keys moves focus to the adjacent tab and immediately sets aria-selected='true', revealing the corresponding tabpanel. In manual tab selection, moving focus with Arrow keys does not change the active panel until the user presses Space or Enter.

distractorNotes.b: In accessible tablists, the Tab key moves into or out of the tabpanel, whereas Left and Right Arrow keys navigate between individual tabs.
distractorNotes.c: Requiring Space or Enter to activate the focused tab describes manual tab selection rather than automatic tab selection.
distractorNotes.d: Automatic tab selection activates the tabpanel upon receiving focus, but leaves keyboard focus on the tab rather than jumping into the panel.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Tabs pattern defines automatic activation as selection following keyboard focus.

stem: According to the WAI-ARIA Tabs pattern, what is the correct tabindex and role configuration for tabs in a horizontal tablist?

options.text: role='tab' on each tab, with tabindex='0' on every tab to allow sequential Tab key access to each tab.
role='tab' on each tab, with tabindex='0' on the active tab and tabindex='-1' on inactive tabs.
role='tab' on each tab, with tabindex='-1' on every tab and tabindex='0' on the tabpanel container.
role='button' on each tab, with tabindex='1' on the active tab and tabindex='0' on inactive tabs.

explanation: The APG Tabs pattern implements a roving tabindex. Only the currently selected tab has tabindex='0', making it the single tab stop when tabbing into the tablist. All inactive tabs have tabindex='-1', allowing users to cycle through tabs using Left and Right Arrow keys without cluttering the page Tab sequence.

distractorNotes.a: Setting tabindex='0' on every tab forces users to Tab through all tabs, violating the APG roving tabindex pattern.
distractorNotes.c: In roving tabindex, the active tab must carry tabindex='0' so keyboard users can navigate into the tablist via Tab.
distractorNotes.d: Tabs require role='tab' rather than role='button', and positive tabindex values disrupt natural document tab order.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Tabs pattern specifies roving tabindex with tabindex 0 on active tab and -1 on inactive tabs.

stem: In an accessible custom tree view widget, what is the required ARIA role hierarchy according to the WAI-ARIA APG Treeview pattern?

options.text: role="menu" > role="menuitem" > role="region"
options.hintText: structures an application command menu with sub-regions

options.text: role="listbox" > role="option" > role="list"
options.hintText: structures a list of selectable items with nested lists

options.text: role="tree" > role="treeitem" > role="group"
options.hintText: structures a hierarchical tree with tree items and expandable groups

options.text: role="grid" > role="row" > role="table"
options.hintText: structures a two-dimensional grid of cells with nested tables

explanation: The APG Treeview pattern requires a container with role='tree'. Immediate items and branch nodes carry role='treeitem'. When a treeitem contains a collapsible set of child items, those children are grouped inside a container with role='group'.

distractorNotes.a: role='menu' and role='menuitem' are reserved for application command menus, not hierarchical tree views.
distractorNotes.b: role='listbox' and role='option' represent flat selection lists, not multi-level hierarchical tree widgets.
distractorNotes.d: role='grid' represents two-dimensional tabular data grids, not hierarchical expandable tree structures.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Treeview pattern defines structure using role tree, treeitem, and nested group elements.

stem: According to the WAI-ARIA APG Treeview pattern, what should occur when keyboard focus is on an expanded parent treeitem and the user presses the Left Arrow key?

options.text: Focus moves up to the parent node of the treeitem without modifying the node expansion state.
Focus shifts immediately into the first child item inside the open group without collapsing it.
Focus moves to the previous sibling treeitem while leaving the current parent treeitem expanded.
The parent treeitem collapses its child branch while keyboard focus remains on that parent treeitem.

explanation: In the APG Treeview pattern, when focus is on an open parent treeitem, pressing the Left Arrow collapses the branch while leaving focus on that item. Pressing Left Arrow when the node is already closed (or on an end child) moves focus to its parent node.

distractorNotes.a: Moving to the parent node occurs when pressing Left Arrow on an already collapsed node or child item, not on an expanded node.
distractorNotes.b: Moving to the first child item occurs when pressing Right Arrow on an expanded node, whereas Left Arrow collapses the node.
distractorNotes.c: Up Arrow navigates to the previous sibling or visible node, while Left Arrow collapses the currently expanded branch.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Treeview pattern defines Left Arrow behavior to collapse open nodes and keep focus on the node.

stem: What is the primary functional difference between implementing an HTML table with role='grid' versus a standard table with role='table'?

options.text: A grid is an interactive widget where arrow keys move focus between cells, whereas a table holds static data.
A grid enables sortable and filterable column headers, whereas a table cannot include interactive controls.
A grid allows screen readers to announce row and column counts, whereas a table suppresses tabular metadata.
A grid is rendered natively by the web browser using CSS Grid, whereas a table requires CSS display table.

explanation: In ARIA, role='grid' designates an interactive widget containing cells that users navigate using directional arrow keys (2D navigation). In contrast, role='table' (and native HTML table) represents static tabular data intended for assistive technology reading and browse modes.

distractorNotes.b: Standard tables can include interactive sorting and filtering buttons; role='grid' is specifically for composite 2D keyboard navigation.
distractorNotes.c: Screen readers announce row and column counts for both tables and grids, making structural announcements identical.
distractorNotes.d: ARIA roles define accessibility semantics and keyboard behavior, completely independent of CSS layout engines.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Grid pattern defines grids as interactive widgets with 2D cell navigation via arrow keys.

stem: When authoring an accessible custom slider using role='slider', when is it necessary to provide the aria-valuetext attribute?

options.text: When the slider minimum and maximum values exceed standard default limits of zero and one hundred.
When the current numeric value does not convey the human-readable meaning, such as representing days of week.
When the slider is rendered vertically on the screen instead of along a horizontal coordinate axis.
When the slider uses decimal or fractional step increments rather than whole positive integer values.

explanation: While aria-valuenow supplies the required programmatic numeric value, aria-valuetext is required whenever the numeric value does not express the true human-readable context (e.g., numeric value 3 representing 'Wednesday' or numeric value 1 representing 'Small').

distractorNotes.a: Custom minimum and maximum values are conveyed using numeric aria-valuemin and aria-valuemax attributes.
distractorNotes.c: Slider orientation is communicated using aria-orientation='vertical', not aria-valuetext.
distractorNotes.d: Decimal step increments are conveyed directly by numeric aria-valuenow and aria-valuestep without requiring valuetext.

sourceNote: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 §6.6 aria-valuetext defines presenting human-readable text when numeric valuenow is inadequate.

stem: According to the WAI-ARIA APG Spinbutton pattern, which keyboard shortcuts decrement and increment the spinbutton value by larger steps?

options.text: Shift + Left Arrow and Shift + Right Arrow
options.hintText: horizontal arrow keys paired with the shift modifier

options.text: Home and End
options.hintText: boundary navigation keys typically moving to minimum and maximum limits

options.text: Page Down and Page Up
options.hintText: paging keys typically mapped to multi-unit navigation or adjustments

options.text: Alt + Down Arrow and Alt + Up Arrow
options.hintText: vertical arrow keys paired with the alt modifier

explanation: In the APG Spinbutton pattern, Up Arrow and Down Arrow adjust the value by single steps. Page Up and Page Down increment and decrement the value by larger predetermined increments (e.g., steps of 10). Home sets the value to the minimum, and End sets it to the maximum.

distractorNotes.a: Shift modifiers with arrow keys are not the APG standard large-step commands for spinbuttons.
distractorNotes.b: Home and End navigate directly to the minimum and maximum allowable values, respectively.
distractorNotes.d: Alt key combinations are reserved for browser shortcuts or operating system accelerator commands.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Spinbutton pattern specifies Page Up and Page Down for large step value adjustments.

stem: According to the WAI-ARIA APG Breadcrumb pattern, what is the recommended semantic markup structure for a breadcrumb trail?

options.text: An aside element with role='tree' wrapping an unordered list where the currently active link has aria-selected='true'.
A div element with role='menu' wrapping anchor links where the active item declares aria-haspopup='menu'.
A section element with aria-roledescription='trail' wrapping span tags separated by slash characters.
A nav element with aria-label='Breadcrumb' wrapping an ordered list where current page has aria-current='page'.

explanation: An accessible breadcrumb uses `<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">` to establish a navigation landmark with a distinct label. An ordered list (`<ol>`) represents the hierarchical trail of links, and `aria-current="page"` marks the link representing the active page.

distractorNotes.a: Breadcrumbs are not trees and should use standard navigation semantics rather than tree roles.
distractorNotes.b: Breadcrumbs are standard links representing page hierarchy, not an application action menu widget.
distractorNotes.c: An ordered list within a labelled nav element is the standardized accessible pattern, not arbitrary spans with custom role descriptions.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Breadcrumb pattern recommends nav with aria-label, ol list, and aria-current page on the last item.

stem: Why does the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide advise against using role='menu' and role='menuitem' for website navigation links?

options.text: It overrides link semantics and disables normal screen reader reading keys in favor of desktop arrow keys.
It breaks visual CSS layout rendering rules by forcing desktop web browsers into native operating system menu styling.
It causes screen readers to suppress link announcements until the user presses an explicit disclosure button.
It restricts navigation items to executing local JavaScript commands rather than navigating to external URLs.

explanation: ARIA menus (role='menu' / 'menubar') are designed to emulate desktop application menus (like desktop File/Edit menus). Applying them to website navigation strips link semantics from screen reader users and requires custom arrow key trapping that breaks standard webpage reading and link discovery behaviors.

distractorNotes.b: ARIA roles alter accessibility tree properties and have no effect on CSS styling or browser rendering engines.
distractorNotes.c: Screen readers can still announce menu items, but they treat them as application commands rather than web hyperlinks.
distractorNotes.d: While ARIA menus emulate desktop application command bars, there is no technical restriction against embedding navigation URLs.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Menubar pattern cautions that menus emulate desktop application menus, not website site navigation.

stem: When implementing a modal dialog, what built-in accessibility behavior does the native HTML dialog element provide when opened with showModal()?

options.text: It renders a non-modal popup that leaves background elements interactive while moving focus to the dialog.
It places the dialog in the top layer, creates a backdrop, and confines keyboard focus to the dialog.
It automatically traps keyboard focus while requiring developers to set aria-hidden on background elements.
It keeps keyboard focus on the opening trigger element until the user explicitly clicks inside the dialog.

explanation: The HTML `<dialog>` element opened via `.showModal()` natively renders in the browser top layer, generates a `::backdrop` pseudo-element, blocks interaction with background elements, and automatically traps keyboard focus within the dialog without custom JavaScript focus traps.

distractorNotes.a: Rendering a non-modal dialog that leaves background content interactive describes dialog.show(), whereas showModal() creates a modal.
distractorNotes.c: showModal() automatically makes background elements inert to assistive technology, removing the need to manually set aria-hidden on siblings.
distractorNotes.d: showModal() automatically moves initial focus into the dialog rather than leaving it on the opening trigger.

sourceNote: HTML specification defines dialog showModal method providing native modal behavior and focus confinement.

stem: In which scenario is role='alertdialog' the appropriate widget role instead of role='dialog'?

options.text: A multi-field registration form asking a new user to enter their name, email, and shipping address.
A photo gallery modal displaying an enlarged thumbnail with next and previous media buttons.
A modal prompt warning that unsaved edits will be permanently lost unless user confirms discarding changes.
A terms and conditions popup containing several scrollable paragraphs of legal text for reference.

explanation: The role alertdialog is reserved for urgent interruptive dialogs that require immediate user response to stop an impending critical condition or irreversible action, such as data loss or session expiration. Standard dialogs use role dialog.

distractorNotes.a: General data entry forms and registration workflows should use role='dialog'.
distractorNotes.b: Image lightboxes and media viewports do not represent critical alerts and should use role='dialog'.
distractorNotes.d: Lengthy reference documents should use role='dialog' to give users control over reading pace without alert interrupts.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Alertdialog pattern specifies alertdialog for urgent dialogs requiring immediate user response.

stem: According to the WAI-ARIA APG Feed pattern, what keyboard interaction enables users to navigate between feed articles efficiently?

options.text: Tab and Shift + Tab
options.hintText: sequential navigation keystrokes moving between focusable controls

options.text: Down Arrow and Up Arrow
options.hintText: directional navigation keys moving between lines or elements

options.text: Spacebar and Enter
options.hintText: keystrokes for standard page scrolling or activating focused controls

options.text: Page Down and Page Up
options.hintText: paging keystrokes moving focus between adjacent articles or sections

explanation: In the APG Feed pattern, feeds can contain infinite scrolling streams. To allow users to move between articles without tabbing through every link or button inside each article, Page Down moves focus to the start of the next article, and Page Up moves focus to the previous article.

distractorNotes.a: Tab moves between interactive elements inside an article or exits the feed; it does not jump between articles.
distractorNotes.b: Up and Down Arrow keys navigate within the content of an article, whereas Page Up and Page Down navigate between articles.
distractorNotes.c: Spacebar triggers native page scroll or button activation rather than structured feed navigation.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Feed pattern specifies Page Down and Page Up for navigating between articles.

stem: How does an accessible toggletip differ from an accessible tooltip in trigger mechanism and screen reader interaction?

options.text: A toggletip opens on click and announces content via live region, while a tooltip appears on hover/focus.
A toggletip moves keyboard focus into the popup container, whereas a tooltip keeps focus on the trigger.
A toggletip uses role='tooltip' referenced by aria-describedby, whereas a tooltip uses role='status'.
A toggletip appears automatically upon page load, whereas a tooltip requires explicit user interaction.

explanation: A tooltip appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus of an interactive control, presenting supplementary information referenced via aria-describedby. A toggletip is an interactive button (disclosure) that the user clicks/presses, outputting its content into a live region or expanded container so assistive technologies announce it without moving focus away.

distractorNotes.b: A toggletip keeps focus on the trigger button and announces content via a live region rather than stealing keyboard focus like a dialog.
distractorNotes.c: Tooltips use role='tooltip' linked via aria-describedby, whereas toggletips typically use disclosure buttons and live regions.
distractorNotes.d: Both tooltips and toggletips require user interaction; neither displays automatically upon initial page load.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Tooltip pattern defines hover/focus tooltips vs interactive click-activated toggletips.

stem: Why is using the native HTML details and summary element combination preferred over custom ARIA disclosure widgets?

options.text: It automatically exposes native heading semantics in the document outline without requiring heading tags.
It provides built-in keyboard toggling, expanded state announcement, and focus handling without JavaScript.
It automatically meets WCAG Level AAA requirements while custom ARIA disclosures are limited to Level AA.
It announces disclosure content updates via an assertive live region without requiring screen reader focus.

explanation: Native `<details>` and `<summary>` elements provide accessible disclosure functionality out of the box: the browser manages keyboard activation (Enter and Space), toggles the open state, and exposes appropriate roles and states to assistive technologies without requiring custom ARIA or JavaScript handlers.

distractorNotes.a: The summary element provides disclosure trigger semantics but does not map to a heading role unless an explicit heading tag is included.
distractorNotes.c: WCAG conformance levels depend on complete accessibility behavior rather than whether native or custom elements are used.
distractorNotes.d: Native details elements do not inject assertive live regions; they expose standard expanded and collapsed states to assistive technology.

sourceNote: HTML specification defines details and summary elements providing native disclosure semantics and interaction.

stem: Under the Accessible Name and Description Computation (AccName 1.2), how are elements with display: none handled when referenced by aria-labelledby?

options.text: They are ignored completely because hidden elements are excluded from all accessibility computations.
They require visibility: hidden instead of display: none to be included in the calculation.
They are traversed and included in the accessible name calculation of the referencing element.
They are included only if the referenced element is an interactive form control or anchor link.

explanation: Under AccName 1.2 Step 2B, if an element is referenced by aria-labelledby (or aria-describedby), the computation algorithm includes the text content of the referenced element even if that referenced element has display: none, visibility: hidden, or aria-hidden='true'.

distractorNotes.a: Hidden elements are included in the name calculation when explicitly referenced by ID in aria-labelledby.
distractorNotes.b: AccName 1.2 Step 2B traverses referenced elements regardless of whether display: none or visibility: hidden is applied.
distractorNotes.d: AccName 1.2 traverses referenced elements regardless of whether they are interactive controls or static text nodes.

sourceNote: W3C AccName 1.2 §4.3 Step 2B specifies including hidden elements when referenced by aria-labelledby.

stem: When an HTML input element contains both an aria-labelledby attribute and an aria-label attribute, which takes precedence in AccName 1.2?

options.text: aria-label
options.hintText: defines an explicit string value labeling an interactive element

options.text: Concatenation of both attributes
options.hintText: joins multiple naming strings separated by a space

options.text: The native label element
options.hintText: provides host language labeling for associated form controls

options.text: aria-labelledby
options.hintText: references elements that provide an accessible name

explanation: Under the Accessible Name and Description Computation 1.2, aria-labelledby has the highest priority (Step 2B) and completely overrides aria-label (Step 2C). aria-label is only evaluated if aria-labelledby is not present or yields an empty name.

distractorNotes.a: aria-label has lower precedence than aria-labelledby and is overridden when aria-labelledby is present.
distractorNotes.b: The calculation chooses the higher-precedence attribute rather than concatenating both strings.
distractorNotes.c: In AccName 1.2, ARIA labeling attributes take precedence over native host language label elements.

sourceNote: W3C AccName 1.2 §4.3 establishes aria-labelledby precedence over aria-label in accessible name computation.

stem: What is the primary functional difference between the aria-describedby and aria-details attributes?

options.text: aria-describedby references flat text descriptions, whereas aria-details points to rich structured content.
aria-describedby is supported on input elements, whereas aria-details is restricted to anchor hyperlinks.
aria-describedby is announced before the accessible name, whereas aria-details is announced before the role.
aria-describedby creates a visual popup tooltip, whereas aria-details opens a modal dialog box on click.

explanation: aria-describedby provides a concise or flat string description that assistive technology reads as a continuous text stream. In contrast, aria-details links to rich, structured content (such as complex data tables, multi-paragraph explanations, or charts) where users can navigate the structure.

distractorNotes.b: Both attributes can be applied to diverse interactive and landmark elements across the DOM.
distractorNotes.c: The accessible name is always computed and announced before descriptions or extended details.
distractorNotes.d: ARIA attributes convey relationships to assistive technologies and do not render visual popups or modals.

sourceNote: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 §6.6 aria-details specifies referencing complex, rich structured descriptions beyond flat text.

stem: What is the most accessible markup pattern for an informative inline SVG graphic conveying complex diagram information?

options.text: aria-hidden='true' on the svg element with an alt attribute containing the full diagram description.
role='img' on the svg element with aria-labelledby referencing IDs of nested title and desc elements.
role='presentation' on the svg element accompanied by a title attribute on nested path elements.
tabindex='0' on the svg element with aria-live='assertive' to announce vector path changes continuously.

explanation: An informative SVG should have role='img' to ensure all browsers and screen readers map it as an image. Providing title and desc elements with unique IDs referenced by aria-labelledby on the svg ensures robust accessible name and description computation.

distractorNotes.a: aria-hidden='true' hides the SVG from assistive technologies, and the SVG element does not support the HTML alt attribute.
distractorNotes.c: role='presentation' removes image semantics, and title attributes on individual vector paths are rarely exposed.
distractorNotes.d: SVGs that are not interactive should not be placed in the tab order, and static diagrams do not require assertive live regions.

sourceNote: W3C SVG 2 §5.4 Title and Desc elements combined with ARIA provide accessible graphics semantics.

stem: How should an inline SVG icon be coded when it is purely decorative and placed next to visible text that already conveys its meaning?

options.text: Add role='figure' and an empty title attribute to ensure screen readers announce an unnamed visual asset.
Add alt='' and tabindex='0' to allow keyboard users to inspect the vector coordinates directly.
Add aria-hidden='true' and focusable='false' to the svg element to remove it from accessibility tree and tab order.
Add aria-label='Decorative Icon' to ensure screen readers explicitly inform the user of the visual icon.

explanation: Purely decorative SVGs should be hidden from assistive technologies using aria-hidden='true'. Adding focusable='false' is also recommended to prevent Internet Explorer / older Edge versions from erroneously adding the SVG to the sequential keyboard tab order.

distractorNotes.a: role='figure' exposes an unnecessary structural container, and empty title attributes do not reliably hide SVGs.
distractorNotes.b: The alt attribute is invalid on SVG elements, and decorative graphics must not receive keyboard focus.
distractorNotes.d: Announcing decorative icons clutters screen reader output with irrelevant information.

sourceNote: W3C Using ARIA §4.1 decorative elements must be hidden from assistive technology using aria-hidden true.

stem: In a complex data table where data cells are associated with multiple non-contiguous headers across multiple levels, which markup technique is required?

options.text: Applying scope='auto' to all th elements and wrapping each distinct data cell inside a thead container.
Using scope='col' and scope='row' on header cells with nested thead containers for each table level.
Applying aria-labelledby on each data cell referencing the ordered ID list of the related header cells.
Assigning unique id attributes to header cells and listing their IDs in headers attributes on data cells.

explanation: For complex tables with multi-level or irregular headers, the scope attribute is often insufficient. HTML specifies using unique id attributes on each th and referencing them in the headers attribute of each td using an ordered, space-separated list of IDs.

distractorNotes.a: scope='auto' is not a valid HTML scope value, and thead cannot be nested inside individual data cells.
distractorNotes.b: Standard scope attributes cannot associate data cells across complex multi-level, non-contiguous header structures.
distractorNotes.c: HTML provides the native headers attribute for complex cell associations; aria-labelledby is not standard on data cells.

sourceNote: HTML specification §4.9.11 defines header and data cell associations using id and headers attributes.

stem: When is the scope='colgroup' attribute properly applied in an accessible HTML data table?

options.text: On a th element that spans across multiple columns using colspan to identify it as a header for that group.
On a td element located in the final summary row to indicate that it aggregates calculations for the table.
On individual th elements in a simple table to inform assistive technologies that styling applies to columns.
On the col element inside a colgroup container to establish keyboard navigation boundaries between cells.

explanation: The scope colgroup attribute is applied to a th header cell that spans multiple columns (typically via colspan) to designate that the header applies to all columns in that group. The scope rowgroup attribute performs the equivalent function for multi-row spanning headers.

distractorNotes.b: The scope attribute is only valid on th elements, not td elements.
distractorNotes.c: Simple column headers apply to a single column and should use scope='col', not scope='colgroup'.
distractorNotes.d: The scope attribute belongs on th elements, not col tags, and scope does not alter keyboard navigation.

sourceNote: HTML specification §4.9.10 defines scope colgroup for table header cells spanning a group of columns.

stem: What built-in keyboard behavior do native HTML button elements provide that custom div elements with role='button' lack by default?

options.text: Native buttons automatically trigger click events upon pressing the Escape key and the Tab key.
Native buttons automatically trigger click events upon pressing both the Enter key and the Spacebar.
Native buttons automatically map Arrow keys to navigate between sibling button controls in a container.
Native buttons trigger click events on Enter, but require custom JavaScript listeners for Spacebar.

explanation: Native HTML button elements trigger their click action when activated via either the Enter key or the Spacebar, and prevent page scrolling on Spacebar. A div with role='button' requires custom JavaScript event listeners for both key codes, plus event.preventDefault() for Spacebar.

distractorNotes.a: The Tab key moves focus and Escape dismisses overlays; neither triggers button click actions.
distractorNotes.c: Arrow keys do not trigger button navigation unless custom widget scripts (like toolbar or roving tabindex) are added.
distractorNotes.d: Native HTML buttons inherently support both Enter and Space activation without custom event listeners.

sourceNote: W3C Using ARIA §2.1 details native button keyboard behaviors including Enter and Space key activation.

stem: What is the functional impact of assigning tabindex='-1' to a container element such as a main content area or section heading?

options.text: The element receives focus during reverse Tab key navigation, but is skipped during forward Tab navigation.
The element is placed at the end of the sequential Tab order after all elements with tabindex='0'.
The element can receive programmatic focus via JavaScript .focus() but is excluded from sequential Tab order.
The element can be focused via the Tab key, but cannot receive programmatic focus through JavaScript .focus().

explanation: Setting tabindex='-1' removes an element from the sequential keyboard navigation order (Tab key navigation) while allowing it to receive focus programmatically using the JavaScript .focus() method. This is essential for routing focus in SPAs or skip link destinations.

distractorNotes.a: tabindex='-1' removes an element from sequential keyboard navigation in both forward and reverse directions.
distractorNotes.b: Elements with tabindex='-1' are excluded entirely from the sequential tab order rather than placed at the end.
distractorNotes.d: tabindex='-1' specifically enables programmatic focus via .focus() while excluding the element from the Tab key sequence.

sourceNote: HTML specification §5.3.3 defines tabindex -1 as programmatically focusable while excluded from sequential tab order.

stem: Why is the use of positive tabindex values (such as tabindex='1' or tabindex='2') considered an accessibility antipattern?

options.text: It restricts keyboard access exclusively to screen readers while disabling standard hardware keyboards.
It causes screen reader virtual cursor navigation to skip the element entirely during reading mode.
It locks keyboard focus on that element and prevents users from tabbing to subsequent interactive controls.
It creates an unpredictable tab order by jumping ahead of native controls, disrupting keyboard navigation.

explanation: Positive tabindex values force the browser to navigate elements in order of increasing tabindex value before visiting standard elements in the natural DOM order. This disrupts logical reading and tab order, creating severe disorientation for sighted keyboard users.

distractorNotes.a: Positive tabindex values do not disable hardware keyboards; they alter the order in which focusable elements are visited.
distractorNotes.b: Screen readers can still access elements with positive tabindex values during virtual cursor reading mode.
distractorNotes.c: Positive tabindex alters navigation order but does not create an inescapable focus trap.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.3 Focus Order guidance explains how positive tabindex disrupts logical navigation order.

stem: What is the primary accessibility purpose of wrapping a group of related radio buttons in a fieldset element with a legend?

options.text: It provides a common group label that screen readers announce when each radio button receives focus.
It ensures that one radio button can be selected at a time across the entire web application.
It converts the radio buttons into a multi-select checkbox group when viewed on mobile screen viewports.
It automatically validates that the user selects an option prior to HTML form submission.

explanation: A fieldset element groups related controls, and its legend provides an accessible group name. When a user tabs into any radio button within the fieldset, screen readers announce both the legend context (such as 'Preferred Shipping Method') and the specific radio button label.

distractorNotes.b: Mutual exclusivity of radio buttons is governed by matching the name attribute on the input elements, not by fieldset.
distractorNotes.c: fieldset provides semantic grouping and does not transform radio controls into checkboxes.
distractorNotes.d: Required validation is enforced via the required attribute or JavaScript validation, not by fieldset.

sourceNote: HTML specification §4.10.16 defines fieldset and legend as providing group context for related form controls.

stem: When client-side form validation detects an error in a text input, what combination of markup practices correctly exposes the error to assistive technologies?

options.text: Setting aria-hidden='true' on the input and moving the error message into the document title element.
Setting aria-invalid='true' on input and referencing error element ID via aria-describedby or aria-errormessage.
Adding CSS class error-border to the input and wrapping the error message in a hidden summary tag.
Setting role='alert' directly on the input element while leaving the original value unchanged.

explanation: To make form validation accessible, developers should set aria-invalid='true' on the invalid form field and link it to the descriptive error text using aria-describedby (or aria-errormessage), ensuring screen reader users hear the specific failure details when focusing the field.

distractorNotes.a: aria-hidden='true' hides the form field from assistive technologies, preventing the user from correcting the error.
distractorNotes.c: CSS visual classes do not convey semantic error states to non-sighted assistive technology users.
distractorNotes.d: Inputs cannot have role='alert'; alert is a container role that overrides native form input semantics.

sourceNote: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 §6.6 aria-invalid and aria-errormessage define exposing form validation error states.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.5 (Identify Input Purpose), what technique satisfies the requirement for form fields collecting user personal information?

options.text: Providing an aria-description attribute containing a dictionary definition of the required data format.
Ensuring the visible label text and input id attribute use standardized strings like 'email' or 'name'.
Applying standard HTML autocomplete attribute tokens corresponding to the input purpose, like autocomplete='email'.
Adding placeholder text and title attributes that describe the personal information field to users.

explanation: WCAG SC 1.3.5 requires that inputs collecting information about the user can be programmatically identified using the HTML autocomplete attribute with specified tokens (such as autocomplete='name', autocomplete='email', or autocomplete='postal-code').

distractorNotes.a: aria-description provides supplementary text but does not enable automated browser autofill or icon identification.
distractorNotes.b: Visible label strings and element IDs do not satisfy the SC 1.3.5 requirement for machine-readable purpose tokens.
distractorNotes.d: Placeholder and title text do not programmatically identify input purpose according to the SC 1.3.5 specification.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose requires appropriate HTML autocomplete attribute values.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication (Minimum)), which implementation violates the requirement for cognitive function tests during login?

options.text: Supporting password managers and browser autofill so users do not have to memorize credentials.
Permitting users to paste their password directly from an external password vault into the password field.
Offering WebAuthn biometric passkey authentication through device facial recognition or fingerprint scanners.
Requiring users to memorize and retype a security code displayed as an image without copy-paste or autofill.

explanation: SC 3.3.8 requires that authentication processes do not rely solely on cognitive function tests (such as memorizing strings or solving puzzles) unless an alternative method, copy-paste support, or object recognition alternative is provided. Blocking copy-paste on random codes violates this criterion.

distractorNotes.a: Supporting password managers and autofill is an explicit conforming technique under SC 3.3.8.
distractorNotes.b: Allowing password copy-paste from clipboards or managers is an explicit conforming technique.
distractorNotes.c: Biometric WebAuthn passkeys are explicitly recognized as an accessible alternative that avoids cognitive tests.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) prohibits unassisted cognitive tests like memorizing text.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.7 (Redundant Entry), what is required when a multi-step checkout process asks for the customer billing address?

options.text: Previously entered shipping address information must be either auto-populated or available for selection.
The user must re-enter the address manually if the application provides a visible progress bar for steps.
The application may require manual re-entry if the user takes longer than five minutes to complete steps.
The user must re-type their full address manually to verify data entry accuracy and confirm address details.

explanation: SC 3.3.7 requires that information previously entered by or provided to the user in the same multi-step process is either auto-populated or available for the user to select, reducing cognitive effort and physical fatigue, unless re-entry is essential (e.g. password verification).

distractorNotes.b: A visible progress indicator does not exempt an application from the redundant entry requirement under SC 3.3.7.
distractorNotes.c: Session timeouts do not exempt multi-step processes from auto-populating or providing selection for previously entered data.
distractorNotes.d: General data accuracy verification is not an allowable exception under SC 3.3.7; information must be auto-populated or selectable.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry requires auto-populating or offering previously entered data.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.7 (Dragging Movements), how must a draggable kanban board or sortable list be designed to conform at Level AA?

options.text: Support keyboard navigation as the sole alternative, without requiring single-pointer drag alternatives.
Provide single-pointer alternatives such as click-activated move buttons or a menu to move items between columns.
Display a visible tooltip showing target coordinate drop zones whenever the user begins a dragging gesture.
Allow users to cancel the drag by pressing the Escape key before releasing the pointer over a drop target.

explanation: SC 2.5.7 requires that all functionality requiring a dragging movement (such as drag-and-drop sorting or slider dragging) can also be operated by a single pointer without dragging (e.g., clickable move buttons, tapping an item then tapping a destination), unless dragging is essential.

distractorNotes.a: Sighted users with motor impairments who use mice or eye tracking cannot drag; SC 2.5.7 specifically mandates single-pointer alternatives.
distractorNotes.c: Visual drop zone indicators do not eliminate the physical dexterity barrier of performing dragging gestures.
distractorNotes.d: Escape cancellation relates to SC 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation, but does not provide a single-pointer non-dragging operational alternative.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements mandates single-pointer non-dragging alternatives.

stem: In a client-side Single Page Application (SPA), what is the most accessible practice when a user navigates to a new view or page?

options.text: Leave keyboard focus on the activated link and rely on visual route animations to show the new view.
Move keyboard focus immediately to the browser URL address bar to reflect the updated route parameter.
Update document title, move focus to the new page main heading or container, and announce transition.
Move keyboard focus directly to the first interactive link located inside the website footer navigation.

explanation: When an SPA navigates to a new route without a full page reload, it must update document.title, move keyboard focus to a logical start point (such as the main landmark or the new view heading equipped with tabindex='-1'), and announce the route change via a polite live region.

distractorNotes.a: Leaving focus on the activated navigation link leaves screen reader and keyboard users without context on the newly rendered view.
distractorNotes.b: Client-side JavaScript cannot programmatically shift DOM focus into browser chrome UI such as the URL address bar.
distractorNotes.d: Jumping focus to the footer skips all newly loaded main page content and disorients the user.

sourceNote: WAI APG and WCAG guidance on SPAs recommend updating document title and focusing primary page heading.

stem: What is the functional effect of setting aria-atomic='true' on an ARIA live region container?

options.text: Assistive technologies announce only the newly added text node while omitting existing sibling text.
Assistive technologies announce updates immediately by interrupting any ongoing speech announcements.
Assistive technologies announce updates only when keyboard focus moves into the live region container.
Assistive technologies announce the entire content of the live region when any change occurs inside it.

explanation: By default (aria-atomic='false'), assistive technologies only announce the specific node or text fragment that changed within a live region. When aria-atomic='true' is declared, assistive technologies present the entire contents of the live region container as a unified whole.

distractorNotes.a: Announcing only the changed node is the default behavior when aria-atomic is set to false.
distractorNotes.b: Interrupting ongoing speech immediately describes aria-live='assertive' rather than aria-atomic='true'.
distractorNotes.c: Live regions announce updates without requiring keyboard focus; aria-atomic controls presentation completeness.

sourceNote: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 §6.6 aria-atomic defines announcing the entire region when changes occur.

stem: In an ARIA live region, what does the configuration aria-relevant='additions removals' instruct assistive technologies to do?

options.text: Announce both newly inserted DOM nodes and nodes that are removed or deleted from the live region.
Announce node additions, but suppress announcements when existing text nodes are modified in place.
Announce changes only when elements are simultaneously added and removed in the same DOM mutation.
Announce node removals only if the user has keyboard focus directly inside the live region wrapper.

explanation: The aria-relevant attribute indicates what types of changes in a live region are relevant and should trigger announcements. The value 'additions removals' specifies that both newly added nodes and deleted nodes should be announced (default is 'additions text').

distractorNotes.b: In-place text modifications are governed by the 'text' token of aria-relevant, not by excluding 'removals'.
distractorNotes.c: aria-relevant triggers announcements whenever any declared mutation type occurs, not only simultaneous compound operations.
distractorNotes.d: aria-relevant informs assistive technology speech queues regardless of whether the user has focused the container.

sourceNote: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 §6.6 aria-relevant specifies which DOM node additions or removals trigger announcements.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.12 (Text Spacing), content must not lose readability or functionality when users apply which minimum letter spacing override?

options.text: Letter spacing (tracking) to at least 0.16 times the font size.
Letter spacing (tracking) to at least 0.12 times the font size.
Letter spacing (tracking) to at least 1.50 times the font size.
Letter spacing (tracking) to at least 2.00 times the font size.

explanation: WCAG SC 1.4.12 specifies four text spacing metrics that content must support without clipping or overlap: line height to at least 1.5x font size, spacing following paragraphs to at least 2x font size, letter spacing (tracking) to at least 0.12x font size, and word spacing to at least 0.16x font size.

distractorNotes.a: 0.16 times the font size corresponds to the word spacing requirement under SC 1.4.12, not letter spacing.
distractorNotes.c: 1.50 times the font size corresponds to the line-height requirement under SC 1.4.12, not letter spacing.
distractorNotes.d: 2.00 times the font size corresponds to the paragraph spacing requirement under SC 1.4.12, not letter spacing.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing defines letter spacing override test threshold of at least 0.12 times font size.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.13 (Content on Hover or Focus), what condition must be satisfied if additional content appears on pointer hover?

options.text: The content may disappear immediately when the pointer leaves the trigger, even if moving toward it.
The content must remain visible for at least 5.0 seconds regardless of subsequent user mouse movements.
The user must be able to move the pointer directly over the new content without it disappearing.
The content must be dismissible solely through the Tab key without providing pointer or Escape options.

explanation: SC 1.4.13 specifies three rules for content that appears on hover or focus: Dismissible (can be dismissed without moving pointer, e.g. via Escape), Hoverable (the pointer can be moved over the additional content without it vanishing), and Persistent (remains visible until dismissed or trigger removed).

distractorNotes.a: Allowing content to disappear when moving toward it violates the 'Hoverable' requirement of SC 1.4.13.
distractorNotes.b: Setting an arbitrary timer does not satisfy SC 1.4.13; content must be persistent until hover is removed or dismissed.
distractorNotes.d: SC 1.4.13 requires content to be dismissible without moving pointer or keyboard focus, such as via the Escape key.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus requires additional content to be dismissible, hoverable, and persistent.

stem: What is the fundamental requirement of WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7 (Focus Visible) for keyboard navigation?

options.text: Every focused control must display an author-customized focus indicator rather than user agent defaults.
The focus indicator must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against all adjacent background colors.
The keyboard focus indicator must have an area at least as large as a 2 CSS pixel perimeter rectangle.
Any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible.

explanation: SC 2.4.7 requires that whenever an interactive element receives keyboard focus, a visible focus indicator must be present so that sighted keyboard users can determine which element currently has focus. Completely removing focus rings (e.g. outline: none without replacement) fails this criterion.

distractorNotes.a: Unstyled default browser focus indicators satisfy SC 2.4.7 provided they are visible when controls receive focus.
distractorNotes.b: 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors is a requirement of Level AAA SC 2.4.13 (Focus Appearance), not Level A SC 2.4.7.
distractorNotes.c: Minimum indicator area is a requirement of Level AAA SC 2.4.13 and Level AA SC 2.4.11, not Level A SC 2.4.7.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible requires a visible keyboard focus indicator on all operable controls.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.13 (Focus Appearance), what contrast ratio must the focus indicator have against adjacent colors?

options.text: At least 3:1 between focused and unfocused states, and at least 3:1 against adjacent non-focus colors.
At least 4.5:1 against inner text color and at least 7:1 against outer background canvas color.
At least 1.5:1 against element borders and at least 2:1 against surrounding white margins.
At least 4.5:1 between focused and unfocused states, and at least 4.5:1 against adjacent colors.

explanation: SC 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (Level AAA) specifies that the focus indicator must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states, as well as at least 3:1 against adjacent non-focus indicator colors.

distractorNotes.b: 4.5:1 and 7:1 are text contrast thresholds from SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.6, not focus indicator contrast metrics.
distractorNotes.c: 1.5:1 and 2:1 fall below the required 3:1 threshold for non-text focus visibility.
distractorNotes.d: 4.5:1 is the Level AA threshold for normal body text under SC 1.4.3, whereas SC 2.4.13 specifies a 3:1 contrast ratio.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.13 Focus Appearance requires at least 3:1 contrast against unfocused states and adjacent colors.

stem: In an HTML5 video player, what is the technical difference between a WebVTT track with kind='captions' versus kind='subtitles'?

options.text: Captions are burned directly into video pixels, while subtitles are delivered via external text files.
Captions include dialogue and sound effects in the video language, while subtitles translate dialogue.
Captions provide translated dialogue for foreign audiences, while subtitles transcribe audio effects.
Captions are spoken aloud by screen readers, whereas subtitles are displayed visually on the screen.

explanation: WebVTT track with kind='captions' is intended for users who are deaf or hard of hearing; it provides transcription of speech along with important non-speech audio information (music, laughter, door slamming) in the audio language. Track with kind='subtitles' provides translated dialogue for viewers who can hear but do not understand the spoken language.

distractorNotes.a: Both captions and subtitles can be provided as external timed text files using the HTML5 track element.
distractorNotes.c: This inverts the definitions: captions transcribe the native language audio and effects, while subtitles translate dialogue.
distractorNotes.d: Both captions and subtitles are visual on-screen text displays; spoken caption synthesis is not standard browser behavior.

sourceNote: HTML specification §4.8.11 defines track kinds: captions for dialogue and sound effects vs subtitles for translation.

stem: What is the primary purpose of providing an Audio Description track for a pre-recorded educational video?

options.text: To replace original spoken dialogue with synthesized speech in a foreign secondary language.
To read the full verbatim text of captions aloud simultaneously with on-screen dialogue.
To narrate essential visual actions, gestures, and scene changes during natural pauses in dialogue.
To display real-time scrolling closed transcript text at the bottom edge of the presentation slide.

explanation: Audio Description (WCAG SC 1.2.3 and 1.2.5) provides verbal narration of key visual details that cannot be understood from the main audio track alone—such as character movements, facial expressions, on-screen text, and scene transitions—spoken during natural pauses in dialogue.

distractorNotes.a: Audio description supplements existing dialogue rather than replacing it with translations.
distractorNotes.b: Audio description narrates visual information, rather than reading closed caption dialogue that is already spoken.
distractorNotes.d: Scrolling text represents captions or subtitles, not an audio description narration track.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded) defines narrating visual actions during dialogue pauses.

stem: In the Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG) 2.0, what fundamental distinction separates Part A from Part B?

options.text: Part A mandates automated accessibility repair algorithms, while Part B specifies manual author checklists.
Part A governs accessible content generation, while Part B governs accessibility of authoring tool UI.
Part A applies to authoring tools for web pages, while Part B applies to non-web document authoring tools.
Part A governs accessibility of authoring tool UI, while Part B governs supporting accessible output.

explanation: ATAG 2.0 is divided into two primary parts: Part A ensures that the authoring tool user interface itself is accessible to authors with disabilities (following WCAG principles). Part B ensures that the tool supports and guides authors in generating accessible web content and preserves accessibility information during transformations.

distractorNotes.a: ATAG 2.0 Part A and Part B address tool UI accessibility and content creation support respectively, not automated vs manual checks.
distractorNotes.b: This inverts the structure: Part A governs tool user interface accessibility, while Part B governs supporting accessible output.
distractorNotes.c: Both Part A and Part B apply to authoring tools across web content, non-web documents, and software applications.

sourceNote: W3C ATAG 2.0 §1.2 defines Part A (accessible authoring tool UI) and Part B (supporting production of accessible content).

stem: Under ATAG 2.0 Guideline B.1, what must an authoring tool do when providing pre-authored content templates to users?

options.text: Ensure that templates provided by the tool are accessible and demonstrate conforming accessibility practices.
Convert all author-supplied custom templates into plain-text formats before publishing to the web.
Ensure that all provided templates conform to WCAG Level AAA regardless of author configuration options.
Require authors to manually remediate template accessibility barriers before creating a new page document.

explanation: ATAG 2.0 Guideline B.1 requires that authoring tools support the production of accessible content. Success Criterion B.1.1.1 mandates that where authoring tools provide pre-authored templates, accessible templates are provided and prominently identified.

distractorNotes.b: ATAG promotes accessible rich media and semantic HTML templates, rather than stripping content down to plain text.
distractorNotes.c: ATAG 2.0 Guideline B.1 targets accessible content aligned with Level AA baseline requirements rather than mandatory Level AAA.
distractorNotes.d: The authoring tool itself must supply accessible templates rather than placing the remediation burden on the end author.

sourceNote: W3C ATAG 2.0 Guideline B.1 specifies authoring tools must provide accessible templates to authors.

stem: In the European accessibility standard EN 301 549, how does Clause 9.6 define the conformance requirements for web pages?

options.text: Web pages are exempt from WCAG conformance if they provide a toll-free customer support telephone number.
Web pages must satisfy all five WCAG 2.1 conformance requirements at Level AA.
Web pages must satisfy only the Perceivable and Operable principles while skipping Understandable criteria.
Web pages must achieve full WCAG 2.1 Level AAA conformance across all public and commercial domains.

explanation: EN 301 549 Clause 9.6 ('WCAG conformance requirements') explicitly requires web pages to meet all five WCAG 2.1 conformance requirements (Conformance Level, Full pages, Complete processes, Only Accessibility-Supported Ways of Using Technologies, and Non-Interference) at Level AA.

distractorNotes.a: Telephone support does not excuse web content from meeting European digital procurement accessibility standards.
distractorNotes.c: All four principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) are mandatory under EN 301 549.
distractorNotes.d: Conformance is pegged to Level AA; Level AAA is not a mandatory baseline under EN 301 549.

sourceNote: ETSI EN 301 549 Clause 9.6 adopts WCAG 2.1 Level AA conformance requirements for web pages.

stem: When creating an accessible modal dialog using ARIA, what is the effect of applying aria-modal='true' to the dialog container?

options.text: It centers the dialog box visually in the middle of the browser viewport with CSS flexbox.
It automatically traps keyboard Tab focus within the dialog without requiring JavaScript focus listeners.
It informs assistive technologies that content outside the dialog container is inert and not navigable.
It automatically applies CSS display none to all background sibling DOM containers on the webpage.

explanation: Declaring aria-modal='true' communicates to assistive technologies that the element is a modal window, directing them to treat content outside the dialog as inert and suppress navigation to elements in the background DOM.

distractorNotes.a: CSS styling rules handle visual centering; ARIA attributes have no visual layout styling effect.
distractorNotes.b: aria-modal tells assistive technology that background content is inert, but it does not trap native keyboard Tab focus.
distractorNotes.d: ARIA attributes modify accessibility tree properties and do not manipulate CSS display styles on sibling DOM elements.

sourceNote: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 §6.6 aria-modal tells assistive technology background content is inert.

stem: According to the WAI-ARIA APG Dialog (Modal) pattern, what focus management action must occur when the user presses Escape inside a modal?

options.text: Keyboard focus must be left on the body element to allow users to navigate from the start of the page.
Keyboard focus must be moved to the primary skip-navigation link located at the top of the document.
The modal closes and keyboard focus jumps to the very last focusable button in the document footer.
The modal closes and keyboard focus is restored to the interactive control that opened the dialog.

explanation: In the APG Modal Dialog pattern, pressing Escape closes the modal, and keyboard focus must be deliberately restored to the interactive control that opened the dialog (the trigger element). Failing to restore focus drops keyboard users back to the start of the page.

distractorNotes.a: Leaving focus on the body disorients keyboard users by dropping them at the page root rather than where they were working.
distractorNotes.b: Moving focus to a skip link resets page navigation instead of returning the user to their prior task context.
distractorNotes.c: Jumping focus to the footer skips the context where the user was working before opening the modal.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Modal Dialog pattern requires restoring focus to the trigger element on close.

stem: What occurs during accessible name computation when an input element declares aria-labelledby='firstNamePrefix firstNameInput'?

options.text: The text content of both referenced elements is concatenated in specified order, separated by a space.
The browser marks the attribute invalid and falls back to using the placeholder attribute.
Only the text of the first referenced ID is used, while subsequent IDs are completely ignored.
The browser concatenates the text of both elements directly without inserting space delimiters.

explanation: Under AccName 1.2, aria-labelledby accepts a space-separated list of element IDs. The accessible name computation algorithm traverses each referenced ID in the specified order and concatenates their computed text alternatives, inserting a single space between them.

distractorNotes.b: Space-separated ID lists are standard valid ARIA syntax and fully supported by AccName 1.2.
distractorNotes.c: All referenced elements in the list are processed and combined in order.
distractorNotes.d: AccName 1.2 Step 2B explicitly specifies inserting a single space separator when concatenating multiple referenced elements.

sourceNote: W3C AccName 1.2 §4.3 Step 2B defines concatenating multiple referenced IDs separated by spaces.

stem: What is the most robust and standard method in semantic HTML for associating visible text with a form input element?

options.text: Wrapping the input element in a p tag with an aria-labelledby attribute matching the p tag class name.
Using a label element whose for attribute exactly matches the id attribute of the input element.
Placing the text in an adjacent span tag and relying on visual proximity in the CSS layout.
Adding a title attribute to the input element that contains the identical text string as nearby text.

explanation: Using `<label for="inputId">` paired with `<input id="inputId">` provides explicit semantic association in HTML. It exposes the accessible name to all assistive technologies and expands the clickable target area so clicking the label focuses the input.

distractorNotes.a: aria-labelledby requires element IDs, not class names, and native label elements are preferred over ARIA on p tags.
distractorNotes.c: Visual proximity does not establish a programmatic association in the accessibility tree.
distractorNotes.d: title attributes do not provide persistent visible labels or expand clickable hit targets.

sourceNote: HTML specification §4.10.4 defines explicit label association using for and id attributes.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Reflow), what technical viewport constraint must a web layout satisfy without requiring two-dimensional scrolling?

options.text: Content must reflow without loss of information or functionality at a width of 1024 CSS pixels.
Content must display all multi-column data tables side-by-side at a resolution of 480 CSS pixels.
Content must reflow without loss of information or functionality at a width of 320 CSS pixels.
Content must disable CSS media queries when the user zooms in browser settings beyond normal zoom.

explanation: SC 1.4.10 Reflow requires that content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions, for vertical scrolling content at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels (equivalent to 400% zoom on a 1280px screen).

distractorNotes.a: 1024 CSS pixels is a desktop/tablet breakpoint, far wider than the required 320 CSS pixel benchmark.
distractorNotes.b: Multi-column tables may require 2D scrolling if two dimensions are essential to the information, but tables are not forced side-by-side.
distractorNotes.d: Media queries are the primary mechanism used to achieve responsive reflow, not disabled.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 Reflow requires responsive layout down to 320 CSS pixels without 2D scrolling.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.8 (Target Size (Minimum)), what is the baseline requirement for interactive pointer target dimensions?

options.text: The target has a size of at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels across all Level A and Level AA success criteria.
The target has a size of at least 12 by 12 CSS pixels provided it contains a high-contrast visual icon.
The target occupies at least five percent of the total available viewport height on touch mobile devices.
The target has a size of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except where spacing or inline exceptions apply.

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (Level AA) requires pointer targets to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or to have sufficient spacing offset such that a 24px diameter circle centered on the target does not intersect another target. SC 2.5.5 is Level AAA and requires 44x44 CSS pixels.

distractorNotes.a: 44 by 44 CSS pixels is the Level AAA target size requirement under SC 2.5.5, not the Level AA baseline of SC 2.5.8.
distractorNotes.b: 12 by 12 CSS pixels falls well below the 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum requirement of SC 2.5.8.
distractorNotes.c: Target size requirements are defined in absolute CSS pixel measurements, not percentage viewport height ratios.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) sets 24 by 24 CSS pixels as the minimum baseline target size.

stem: In an accessible accordion widget, what technique ensures that collapsed accordion panels are completely hidden from assistive technologies?

options.text: Hiding the collapsed panel container using the HTML hidden attribute or CSS display: none.
Setting opacity: 0 and pointer-events: none on the panel container while leaving it in DOM flow.
Adding aria-live='polite' to the collapsed panel container while setting font-size: 0px.
Applying tabindex='0' and aria-disabled='true' to interactive elements inside the collapsed panel.

explanation: Collapsed accordion panels must be completely hidden from both visual presentation and the accessibility tree using hidden or display: none (or visibility: hidden). Using opacity: 0 keeps the content and its focusable children in the tab order and accessibility tree.

distractorNotes.b: opacity: 0 hides content visually but leaves it reachable by screen readers and keyboard tabbing.
distractorNotes.c: aria-live with zero font-size does not remove content from the accessibility tree.
distractorNotes.d: Leaving elements in the panel with tabindex='0' forces keyboard users to navigate through hidden content.

sourceNote: W3C WAI ARIA APG Accordion pattern specifies hiding collapsed panels using hidden or display none.

stem: When implementing a combobox using aria-activedescendant, where does DOM keyboard focus remain while navigating popup options?

options.text: DOM keyboard focus shifts to the individual option elements as the user presses the Down Arrow key.
DOM keyboard focus remains on the combobox input while aria-activedescendant references the option ID.
DOM keyboard focus moves to the document body element while the virtual screen reader cursor inspects the listbox.
DOM keyboard focus is cleared completely until the user presses Enter to confirm their selection.

explanation: With aria-activedescendant, DOM keyboard focus stays on the composite parent control (the input element). As the user navigates using arrow keys, JavaScript updates aria-activedescendant='optionId' to tell assistive technology which option is currently active, without moving DOM focus.

distractorNotes.a: Shifting physical DOM focus to option elements is the roving tabindex approach, not aria-activedescendant.
distractorNotes.c: Focus is never ejected to the body element during composite widget navigation.
